newsitem.title: ST VINCENT: W. Va. couple goes on trial for Caribbean murder.
newsitem.headline: W. Va. couple goes on trial for Caribbean murder.

text.p: James and Penny Fletcher came to the southeastern Caribbean expecting a vacation idyll aboard their luxurious yacht, the "Carefree."

But instead of sailing in paradise, the wealthy West Virginia couple were arrested and charged with the murder of a water-taxi driver. After spending eight months in grim island prisons, they are scheduled to go on trial on Wednesday.

James Fletcher, former president of a Huntington, West Virginia, mining equipment company, and his wife reached the waters off Bequia, a jewel-like island near St. Vincent, in August. Locals said they had at least one public fight, went on spending sprees and were not always entirely sober.

So when water-taxi operator Jerome "Jolly" Joseph was found shot to death after the Fletchers befriended him last fall, islanders immediately pointed fingers at the couple with the fancy boat, calling the killing a crime of passion over an affair between Mrs. Fletcher and Joseph.

Joseph, 30, had worked the turquoise waters around Bequia for years, ferrying tourists from their boats to the island, a prime sailing destination. On Oct. 6 he picked up the Fletchers for a late dinner.

It was the last time he was seen before his bullet-pierced body was fished out of the water on Oct. 9. The Fletchers were arrested for first-degree murder three weeks later and placed in separate prisons in Kingstown. They have been behind bars ever since, their health reportedly failing.
President Bill Clinton asked in May that the couple receive due process under the law.

"It is highly unlikely that the Fletchers can get a fair trial in St. Vincent," Sandra Ingram, a consular officer from the U.S. Embassy in Barbados, said in a report after a preliminary hearing in February and March. She wrote that the case could be summed up by the cross-examination of Ernest James, the lead investigator in the case:

"He admitted that when he charged the Fletchers with murder he had not found the gun, he did not have a ballistics report, he did not have a blood report, he did not have a confession, he did not have an eyewitness, nor did he have fingerprint evidence linking the Fletchers with the crime."

But St. Vincent's government has refused to yield and the wealthy, white couple will be judged by a jury decidedly not of their peers -- not only of a different race and nationality but of a vastly different economic background. If convicted, they face death by hanging at the gallows kept hidden at a hilltop fort overlooking the sparkling Caribbean Sea.

The months behind bars have taken their toll. James Fletcher, 49, has lost 35 pounds in Her Majesty's Prison, a damp, vastly overcrowded stone relic built in 1872. Penny Fletcher, 35, has been plagued by health problems behind bars.
"This whole thing is going to be over soon because I'm not going to make it much longer," James Fletcher said in an interview before St. Vincent cut off media access.
But most islanders seem set against the Fletchers. Prime Minister James "Son" Mitchell summed up public sentiment last month when he called the Fletchers "classic ugly Americans."

U.S. efforts on the Fletchers' behalf may have backfired. The United States is not popular in St. Vincent because of dwindling foreign aid and Clinton's opposition to the Caribbean's preferential access to the European banana market.
Three generations of the Fletcher family will travel to St. Vincent to attend the trial and said they were placing their hopes on the fairness of the jury.
"Jim and Penny didn't act the way they should have there, and they definitely drank too much, but that doesn't mean they killed anyone," Fletcher's sister, Sally Duncan, said.
